What it means: The contribution one group makes to the standard enthalpy of formation. It is the number on each button in the calculator, in kJ/mol.

A term added once per ring or per interaction rather than once per atom. Corrections carry what group additivity cannot see on its own: ring strain, a gauche interaction, two substituents crowding each other across a double bond.

The free-energy cost of a substituent sitting axial rather than equatorial on a cyclohexane ring. A larger A-value means a stronger preference for the equatorial position — a tert-butyl group, at about 20 kJ/mol, is almost never axial.
Standard enthalpy of formation: the enthalpy change on forming one mole of a substance from its elements in their standard states. This is what the group increments and corrections sum to.
Standard Gibbs free energy change. The cyclohexane A-values are free energies, not enthalpies, which is why the calculator will not head a total ΔHf° once one of them is in the sum.
An atom or group written in brackets in a group name, describing what the central atom is bonded to. A ligand is not counted as an atom of the molecule; hydrogen is the exception.
The polyvalent atom a group is built around — the part of the name before the dash.
A value the source published as a span rather than a single number, such as 2.51-4.35. The calculator sums the midpoint and shows the span beside it.
Kilojoules per mole, the unit every value in this calculator is stored in.
Kilocalories per mole. Shown alongside kJ/mol for comparison with older literature; 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.
